name: The FLP Impossibility
statement: In a fully asynchronous system, no deterministic protocol can guarantee agreement if even one process might crash.
statementAccent: no deterministic protocol can guarantee agreement
meaning: The FLP impossibility result, named for Fischer, Lynch, and Paterson, states that in a fully asynchronous distributed system, one with no bounds on message delay or processing speed, there is no deterministic algorithm that can guarantee consensus if even a single process may fail by crashing. Consensus means getting all non-faulty processes to agree on a value, and it must satisfy agreement, validity, and termination together. FLP shows those three cannot all be guaranteed under asynchrony with one crash fault. It is one of the deepest impossibility results in distributed computing and shapes the design of every real consensus system.
mechanism: The obstacle is that in a purely asynchronous system a crashed process cannot be distinguished from one that is merely slow, since there are no timing bounds, so no protocol can safely wait forever for a possibly failed process nor proceed without it. The proof formalises this through valence: a configuration is bivalent if both decision outcomes are still reachable and univalent if only one is. FLP shows an initial bivalent configuration must exist and that from any bivalent configuration an adversary can always delay a single message to keep the system bivalent, yielding an infinite execution that never decides. The property sacrificed is termination: safety can be preserved, but guaranteed liveness cannot.

examples.text: A process that has stopped responding might be dead or merely slow, and with no timing bounds no protocol can tell, so it can neither wait safely nor move on safely.

Real consensus protocols circumvent FLP by adding partial-synchrony timing assumptions; they always preserve safety and guarantee progress only when timing is favourable, such as with a stable leader.
Ben-Or's randomised consensus protocol sidesteps FLP by dropping determinism, terminating with probability one, since the impossibility applies only to deterministic algorithms.

variants.name: Partial synchrony
variants.text: Dwork, Lynch, and Stockmeyer showed consensus becomes solvable when message delays are eventually bounded, even if the bound is unknown, the basis of most practical protocols.

variants.name: Failure detectors
variants.text: Chandra and Toueg showed that unreliable failure detectors, which eventually suspect crashed processes, suffice to solve consensus, another route around the impossibility.

whyItMatters: FLP is a foundational impossibility result that draws a hard boundary around what distributed systems can achieve, and it shapes the design of essentially every real consensus system, from replicated databases and state machines to blockchains. By showing that guaranteed consensus is impossible under pure asynchrony with even one crash, it forces every practical protocol to add something, timing assumptions, randomness, or failure detection, in order to gain liveness while never sacrificing safety. Understanding FLP is understanding why systems like Paxos and Raft are built the way they are, and why they promise safety always but progress only under favourable conditions.

working.text: recognise that in a fully asynchronous system with a possible crash, no deterministic protocol can guarantee both safety and termination.
to build a real consensus system, relax the model with partial synchrony, randomness, or a failure detector, restoring the ability to make progress.
design so that agreement and validity hold under all conditions, conceding only that progress may stall when timing is adversarial.

limits: FLP is an impossibility of guaranteed termination in the worst case under a specific model, not a claim that consensus fails in practice, since working systems solve it routinely. The result is narrow and precise, applying only under the conjunction of a deterministic protocol, a fully asynchronous model, a requirement of guaranteed termination, and at least one crash fault; relaxing any one of these restores solvability. It concerns crash, or fail-stop, faults, the mildest kind, which is what makes the impossibility so strong, since harder Byzantine faults inherit it.
misreadings: FLP does not say consensus is impossible in practice; real protocols such as Paxos, Raft, and Byzantine fault-tolerant systems achieve it every day. The result applies only under the full conjunction of deterministic, fully asynchronous, guaranteed-termination, and at least one crash fault, and relaxing any single condition restores solvability. What it forbids is guaranteed termination, not safety, so protocols preserve agreement and validity and give up only guaranteed progress under adversarial timing. And it concerns crash faults, the mildest failure type, not just Byzantine ones.
origin: Proved by Michael Fischer, Nancy Lynch, and Michael Paterson in their 1985 paper 'Impossibility of Distributed Consensus with One Faulty Process' in the Journal of the ACM, which won the Dijkstra Prize.

sources.text: Fischer, Lynch & Paterson, 'Impossibility of Distributed Consensus with One Faulty Process,' Journal of the ACM 32(2):374-382 (1985). — the impossibility result and its conditions.
